title: Full Grown: The Company That Grows Furniture on Trees
summary:
Most furniture is made in factories: trees are cut into boards, then shaped and assembled. But in Derbyshire, England, Gavin and Alice Munro are doing something completely different. Their company, Full Grown, uses a technique called "tree shaping" to grow furniture from living trees.

The process starts by planting young trees and letting them grow for about five years. Then the trees are cut back to their stumps to encourage new shoots — a method called coppicing. The new branches are trained around custom-built metal frames and gradually bent into the shape of chairs, tables, and other pieces. The branches are also grafted, or joined together, so they grow into one solid structure. Once a piece has fully grown, it is harvested and left to dry for about a year. Finally, it is sanded and polished into a smooth, functional piece of furniture.

The Munros mainly work with willow, but they also grow furniture from oak, ash, cherry, and apple trees. Tree-grown furniture takes years to make, but it is very environmentally friendly. Full Grown estimates that its process uses only about 25 percent of the energy needed to produce a wooden chair in a typical factory. Also, no heavy machinery is needed — just sunlight, soil, water, and time. An added bonus? The "Furniture Field" serves as a sanctuary for birds and local wildlife.

Tree shaping is not a new idea. Ancient Greeks, Egyptians, and Chinese used similar methods to create practical and decorative structures. But the Munros, who founded Full Grown in 2006, have taken the idea in a new direction by using the technique to grow functional furniture on a larger scale.

Not surprisingly, Full Grown's unusual creations have attracted attention around the world. Because each piece is unique, the furniture is considered a work of art. It has been displayed in museums and exhibitions in Europe, Asia, and the United States. Several museums have even bought pieces for their permanent collections.

Gavin and Alice next hope to share what they have learned with others through the Full Grown Academy. Scheduled to launch soon, the online courses hope to inspire a new generation to create sustainable, long-lasting furniture.
why_it_matters: Grown furniture asks a bigger question that today's teenagers will have to answer: how much energy and raw material should everyday objects cost, and whether slow, long-lasting goods can compete with cheap mass production.

background_read: Derbyshire (a county in the middle of England, known for its hills and old woodlands) is where Gavin and Alice Munro (the British couple who founded Full Grown in 2006) run their "Furniture Field".

Tree shaping itself is ancient: people have trained living plants for centuries, and in north-east India farmers in Meghalaya grow "living root bridges" by guiding tree roots across rivers so that the bridges become stronger as they age.

In Europe, coppicing — cutting trees back so they send up fresh stems — has been used in woodlands for thousands of years because it gives a steady supply of poles and firewood without killing the tree.

Ordinary furniture making works very differently: most wooden furniture is cut from mature trees, dried in heated kilns, then glued and screwed together, which uses a lot of energy as well as material.

Grown furniture reverses that process, but it has a cost: each piece can take many years to produce, so the result is closer to a sculpture than to a mass-produced product — a slow answer to a throwaway culture in which cheap furniture is often dumped after a few years.

perspectives.description: Supporters see Full Grown as proof that manufacturing does not have to mean smoke, factories and waste. The pieces need only sunlight, soil and time, they lock away carbon while they grow, and the field also shelters birds and other wildlife.

Critics note that a chair which takes many years to grow cannot possibly furnish millions of homes, so it will stay a luxury item for museums and collectors. They also ask whether large-scale tree shaping could take farmland or woodland away from other uses.

Analysts place the company in a long tradition, since ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Chinese already shaped living plants into structures and ornaments. What is new is applying that craft on a commercial scale and selling the results as design objects rather than curiosities.

If the Full Grown Academy teaches the method widely, small workshops and hobbyists could start growing their own pieces, and the idea might spread to other products such as lamp stands or playground structures. The open question is whether the technique can ever be fast enough to matter beyond a niche market.
